summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force on the islands is Dutch national law, applied there in the same form as in the European Netherlands, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No available source describes a provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

The Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27), both visiting residents. Same-sex unions have therefore been registrable in these islands since 2012, and the island registry has performed one for visitors. This 2012 registration is the only dated union event in the sources; no later instance is documented.

Saba's official tourism service documents civil ceremonies running through the island registry, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony and registrar Julieta Woods recorded as flexible about couples' wishes, alongside full destination-wedding suppliers. A couple seeking a civil ceremony on Saba has a documented and functioning route through the registry.
tangentialFactors: GayCities ranked Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, in a list published 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023, citing its standing as part of the Netherlands and that country's anti-discrimination law. The ranking is a travel publication's editorial list rather than an assessment of trans-specific risk, and it names no trans-related provision; it indicates how the island markets itself to equality-minded travellers.
localsOnly: Residents of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba stand under the Dutch anti-discrimination regime as applied to the islands, with no island-level ordinance naming gender identity documented alongside it. The registry practice evidenced on Saba, registering unions for visiting couples, is the same machinery residents use.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced here: gender-marker and passport rules as applied at the islands' airports, screening practice at Flamingo Airport on Bonaire and Juancho E. Yrausquin Airport on Saba, access to facilities, healthcare access for trans visitors, and any hate-crime provision naming gender identity. The marriage and anti-discrimination material does not answer these questions.

No trans-specific incident of violence is documented in the available sources, and no period or denominator is given from which a rate could be derived, so no comparison with the general homicide rate can be made from this material.
